title: AI scams in Georgia and South Florida: How scammers use deepfakes to steal millions

reading.body:
Scammers have deployed AI to impersonate real people, including a South Florida immigration attorney whose identity and voice were cloned to defraud immigrants seeking legal services. The system failure here is social, not technical: voice cloning and deepfake technology operated without the gatekeeping that would normally prevent impersonation, because these tools exist outside any authorization framework. Targets had no reliable way to verify they were communicating with the real attorney rather than a synthetic recreation.

This represents impersonation at scale, enabled by AI tools that can be obtained and used without consent from their subjects. The vulnerability sits upstream of any individual company's deployment: it is the general availability of voice cloning and deepfake creation to anyone, combined with the difficulty of distinguishing synthetic from authentic media in real time. To catch this would have required either restricting access to these tools, or equipping the public with reliable authentication methods before criminals weaponized the technology.

It is not established whether the voice cloning and deepfake tools themselves were purpose-built for fraud or diverted from legitimate uses.

summary:
Scammers are increasingly using artificial intelligence to create deepfakes and clone voices to steal money from victims across Georgia and South Florida. The FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report found that Americans lost nearly $893 million to AI-enabled scams last year. Notable cases include a South Florida immigration attorney whose voice and identity were cloned to target immigrants, and a Cobb County couple who lost approximately $800,000 in a cryptocurrency scam. Overall, the FBI received over 1 million internet crime complaints totaling more than $20 billion in losses.

Florida reported 350 AI-related complaints with $39.9 million in losses, while Georgia had 71 complaints resulting in $10.4 million in losses. Criminals use AI to clone voices from social media, spoof phone numbers, create fake photographs, and research family relationships to make scams more convincing. The Georgia Attorney General recommends families establish private code words to verify identity during emergencies. Experts advise verifying urgent requests through known phone numbers, never sending money based on calls alone, and reporting suspected fraud to local law enforcement and the FBI.
